chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter VII
paragraphs: When an event is taking place, people express their opinions and wishes about it, and since the event results from the collective activity of many people, one of the opinions or wishes expressed is bound to be fulfilled, if only approximately. When one of the opinions expressed is fulfilled, that opinion becomes connected in people's minds with the event as the command that preceded it.

Men are hauling a log. Each expresses his opinion about how and where to haul it. They drag the log away, and it turns out the job was done the way one of them suggested. He gave the order. That is command and power in their most basic form. The man who worked hardest with his hands had less time to think about what he was doing, to reflect on what might come of the common effort, and to give orders. The man who directed most could obviously—because of his greater involvement in directing—work less with his hands.

When a larger group of people directs its activity toward a common goal, there is an even sharper division between those who—because their activity is devoted to directing and commanding—take less direct part in the work itself.

When a person works alone, he always has a set of ideas which, as it seems to him, directed his past activity, justify his present actions, and guide his future plans. Groups of people do the same, allowing those who don't take direct part in the activity to devise rationales, justifications, and plans for the collective effort.

For reasons known or unknown to us, the French began to drown and kill one another. And a corresponding justification appeared in people's belief that this was necessary for the welfare of France, for liberty and equality. People stopped killing one another, and this event was accompanied by the justification that centralized power was needed, resistance to Europe was needed, and so on. People moved from west to east, killing their fellow men, and this event was accompanied by talk about the glory of France, the baseness of England, and so on. History shows us that these justifications for events have no common sense and are self-contradictory—such as the killing of a man as a result of recognizing his rights, and the killing of millions in Russia for the humiliation of England. But these justifications have a necessary function in their own time.

These justifications relieve those who produce the events of moral responsibility. These temporary aims are like the broom attached to the front of a locomotive to sweep snow from the rails: they sweep moral responsibility from people's path.

Without such justifications there would be no answer to the simplest question that arises when examining any historical event: How is it that millions of people commit collective crimes—make war, commit murder, and so on?

Given the complex forms of political and social life in modern Europe, is it possible to imagine any event that is not prescribed, decreed, or ordered by monarchs, ministers, parliaments, or newspapers? Is there any collective action that cannot find its justification in political unity, patriotism, the balance of power, or civilization? So every event that occurs inevitably coincides with some expressed wish and, receiving its justification, is regarded as the product of someone's will.
Whatever direction a ship moves, the parting of the waves it cuts through will always be visible ahead of it. To those on board, the movement of those waves will be the only motion they can perceive.

Only by watching closely, moment by moment, the movement of that parting wave and comparing it with the movement of the ship do we convince ourselves that every ripple is caused by the ship's forward motion, and that we were led astray because we ourselves were imperceptibly moving.

We see the same thing if we watch, moment by moment, the movement of historical figures—that is, if we restore the essential condition of continuity of movement in time—and do not lose sight of the necessary connection between historical persons and the masses.

When the ship moves in one direction, there is one and the same wave ahead of it. When it turns frequently, the wave ahead of it turns frequently too. But wherever it may turn, there will always be a wave running ahead of its movement.

Whatever happens, it always appears that precisely that event was foreseen and decreed. Wherever the ship goes, the rush of water—which neither directs nor increases its movement—foams ahead of it, and from a distance seems not only to move by itself but to govern the ship's course.

Examining only those expressions of will by historical persons which, as commands, were connected with events, historians have assumed that the events depended on those commands. But examining the events themselves and the connection in which the historical persons stood to the people, we have found that historical persons and their commands are dependent on events.
Having reached this conclusion, we can directly and positively answer these two essential questions of history:
(1) What is power?
(2) What force produces the movement of nations?

(1) Power is the relationship of a given person to other individuals, in which the more this person expresses opinions, predictions, and justifications of the collective action being performed, the less he actually participates in that action.

(2) The movement of nations is caused not by power, nor by intellectual activity, nor even by a combination of the two as historians have supposed, but by the activity of all the people who participate in the events—people who always combine in such a way that those taking the largest direct share in the event take the least responsibility for it, and vice versa.

Morally, the wielder of power appears to cause the event; physically, it is those who submit to the power. But since moral activity is inconceivable without physical activity, the cause of the event lies neither in one nor in the other, but in the union of the two.
In other words, the concept of a cause is inapplicable to the phenomena we are examining.

In the final analysis we arrive at the circle of infinity—the ultimate limit that human reason reaches in every domain of thought when it is not merely playing with its subject. Electricity produces heat; heat produces electricity. Atoms attract one another; atoms repel one another.

Speaking of the interaction of heat and electricity, or of atoms, we cannot say why this occurs. We say it is so because it is inconceivable otherwise—because it must be so, because it is a law. The same applies to historical events. Why war and revolution happen we do not know. We only know that to produce one or the other, people form themselves into certain combinations in which all participate; and we say this is so because it is inconceivable otherwise, because it is a law.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: If history dealt only with external phenomena, the establishment of this simple and obvious law would suffice and our argument would be finished. But the law of history relates to man. A particle of matter cannot tell us it does not feel the law of attraction or repulsion, and that the law is untrue. But a man—the subject of history—says plainly: I am free, and therefore not subject to laws.
The presence of the problem of man's free will, though never explicitly stated, is felt at every step in the study of history.

All seriously thinking historians have inevitably confronted this question. All the contradictions, obscurities, and false paths of historical science are due solely to the failure to resolve this question.
If every man's will were free—if each person could act however he pleased—all of history would be a series of disconnected accidents.

If even one man in a million over the course of a thousand years could act freely—that is, as he chose—it is obvious that a single free act by that man, in violation of the laws governing human action, would destroy the possibility of any laws existing for the whole of humanity.
If there is even a single law governing human actions, then free will cannot exist, because then man's will is subject to that law.
In this contradiction lies the problem of free will, which has occupied the greatest human minds since the most ancient times and has always been presented in its full and tremendous significance.

The problem is this: when we observe man as a subject—from whatever point of view, whether theological, historical, ethical, or philosophical—we find a general law of necessity to which he, like everything else that exists, is subject. But when we observe him from within ourselves, as what we are conscious of, we feel ourselves to be free.
This consciousness of self is a source of self-knowledge entirely separate from and independent of reason. Through reason, man observes himself; but only through consciousness does he know himself.
Without consciousness of self, no observation or use of reason is conceivable.

To understand, observe, and draw conclusions, a man must first be conscious of himself as a living being. A man is conscious of himself as living only by the fact that he wills—that is, he is conscious of his own volition. But his will, which constitutes the essence of his life, man can only recognize—and can only recognize—as free.

If, observing himself, a man sees that his will is always directed by one and the same law—whether he observes the necessity of eating, of using his brain, or anything else—he cannot recognize this constant direction of his will otherwise than as a limitation of it. If it were not free, it could not be limited. A man's will seems limited to him precisely because he is conscious of it only as free.
You say: I am not free. But I have raised my hand and let it fall. Everyone understands that this illogical reply is an irrefutable demonstration of freedom.
That reply is the expression of a consciousness that is not subject to reason.

If the consciousness of freedom were not a separate and independent source of self-awareness, it would be subject to reasoning and experience. But in fact, such subjection does not exist and is inconceivable.

A series of experiments and arguments proves to every man that he, as an object of observation, is subject to certain laws, and man accepts this: he never resists the law of gravity or impermeability once he has come to know them. But the same series of experiments and arguments also proves to him that the complete freedom of which he is conscious in himself is impossible, that his every action depends on his constitution, his character, and the motives acting upon him. Yet a man never accepts this.
But while learning just as certainly that his will is subject to laws, he does not and cannot believe it.

No matter how often experiment and reasoning show a man that under the same conditions, with the same character, he will do the same thing as before—yet when he approaches for the thousandth time an action that always ends the same way, he feels just as sure as ever that he can act however he wishes. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experience prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different actions under precisely identical conditions, feels that without this absurd notion—which constitutes the essence of freedom—he cannot imagine life.

He could not live, because all of man's efforts, all his impulses to life, are only efforts to increase freedom. Wealth and poverty, fame and obscurity, power and subjection, strength and weakness, health and disease, education and ignorance, work and leisure, abundance and hunger, virtue and vice are all only greater or lesser degrees of freedom.
A man with no freedom at all cannot be conceived of except as deprived of life.

If the concept of freedom appears to reason as a senseless contradiction—like the possibility of performing two actions at the same instant, or of an effect without a cause—that only proves that consciousness is not subject to reason.

This unshakable, irrefutable consciousness of freedom—uncontrolled by experiment or argument, recognized by all thinkers and felt by everyone without exception—this consciousness without which no concept of man is possible constitutes the other side of the question.
Man is the creation of an all-powerful, all-good, and all-seeing God. What is sin, a concept that arises from the consciousness of human freedom? That is a question for theology.

The actions of men are subject to general, immutable laws expressed in statistics. What is man's responsibility to society, a concept that results from the concept of freedom? That is a question for jurisprudence.

Man's actions proceed from his innate character and the motives acting upon him. What is conscience, and what is the sense of right and wrong in actions that follows from the consciousness of freedom? That is a question for ethics.

Man, in connection with the general life of humanity, appears subject to laws that determine that life. But the same man, apart from that connection, appears to be free. How should the past life of nations and of humanity be regarded—as the result of the free, or of the constrained, activity of men? That is a question for history.

Only in our self-assured age—thanks to that most powerful engine of ignorance, the mass distribution of printed matter—has the question of free will been reduced to a level where the question itself cannot exist. In our time, the majority of so-called advanced thinkers—that is, the crowd of the ignorant—have taken the work of the natural scientists who study one side of the question for a solution of the whole problem.

They say and write and print that the soul and freedom do not exist, that the life of man is expressed by muscular movements, and muscular movements are determined by nervous activity; that the soul and free will do not exist because at some unknown period of time we descended from apes. They say and write and print this not because they suspect that this is what the natural scientists' arguments actually lead to (for you can't cut off a thought in the middle), but because otherwise—if man has no freedom—it would be impossible to live. And man needs to live and to act.

If men descended from apes at some unknown period of time, that is just as comprehensible as that they were made from a handful of earth at a certain period of time (in the first case the unknown is the time; in the second it is the origin). And the question of how man's consciousness of freedom is to be reconciled with the law of necessity to which he is subject cannot be resolved by comparative physiology or zoology, because in frogs, rabbits, and apes we can observe only muscular and nervous activity, while in man we observe both muscular and nervous activity and consciousness.

The naturalists and their followers, who think they can resolve this question, are like plasterers set to plaster one side of a church wall who—taking advantage of the foreman's absence—in an access of zeal plaster over the windows, the icons, the woodwork, and the walls still unfinished, and are delighted that from their plastering point of view everything looks nice and smooth.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter IX
paragraphs: For the resolution of the question of free will or necessity, history has one advantage over other branches of knowledge that deal with this question: for history the question does not concern the essence of man's free will but only its manifestation in the past and under certain conditions.
In this respect, history stands to the other sciences as experimental science stands to abstract science.
The subject of history is not man's will itself, but our picture of it.

And so for history, the insoluble mystery of the incompatibility of free will and necessity does not exist as it does for theology, ethics, and philosophy. History examines a picture of human life in which the union of these two contradictions has already taken place.

In actual life, each historic event and each human action is very clearly and definitely understood without any feeling of contradiction, even though each event presents itself as partly free and partly compulsory.

To solve the question of how freedom and necessity combine, and what constitutes the essence of these two concepts, the philosophy of history can and should follow a path opposite to the one taken by other sciences. Instead of first defining the concepts of freedom and necessity in themselves, and then fitting the facts of life into those definitions, history should derive its definition of the concepts from the enormous quantity of facts at its disposal—studying them as the manifestation of freedom and necessity.
Whatever picture of human activity we consider—whether of many people or one individual—we always see it as partly the result of free will and partly of the law of necessity.

Whether we speak of the migration of peoples and the barbarian invasions, or of Napoleon III's decrees, or of someone's action an hour ago in choosing one direction rather than another for his walk, we feel no contradiction. The degree of freedom and necessity governing each person's actions appears clearly defined to us.

Our sense of the degree of freedom often varies depending on the viewpoint from which we regard the event, but every human action appears to us as a certain combination of freedom and necessity. In every action we examine, we see a certain measure of freedom and a certain measure of necessity. And always, the more freedom we see in any action, the less necessity; and the more necessity, the less freedom.
The proportion of freedom to necessity decreases and increases depending on the viewpoint from which we regard the action, but the relationship is always one of inverse proportion.

A drowning man who grabs another and drags him under; a hungry mother exhausted from nursing who steals food; a soldier trained in discipline who kills a defenseless man on orders—these all seem less guilty, less free, and more subject to the law of necessity, to anyone who knows the circumstances of their actions. And conversely, a man who commits murder out of jealousy with no apparent provocation seems more free and less subject to the law of necessity. In every case, our idea of freedom and necessity depends on the circumstances under which the action took place.
Religion, the common sense of mankind, the science of jurisprudence, and history itself all understand this relationship between necessity and freedom in the same way.
All cases without exception in which our sense of freedom and necessity is increased or diminished depend on three factors:
(1) The relationship of the person who committed the act to the external world.
(2) His relationship to time.
(3) His relationship to the causes that led to the action.

The first factor is the clarity of our perception of the person's relationship to the external world, and the greater or lesser clarity with which we understand his specific position in relation to everything around him. This is what makes it obvious that a drowning man is less free and more subject to necessity than a man standing on dry land. This is why the actions of a man living in close connection with other people in a densely populated area, the actions of a man bound by family, work, or business obligations, are undoubtedly considered less free and more subject to necessity than those of a man living in isolation and solitude.

If we consider a man entirely alone, with no connection to anything around him, each of his actions seems free. But if we see even the slightest connection to anything external—a person he talks to, a book he reads, the work he does, even the air he breathes or the light that falls on the things around him—we see that each of these factors has an influence on him and controls at least some aspect of his activity. And to the extent we see these influences, our sense of his freedom diminishes and our sense of the necessity he is subject to increases.

The second factor is the more or less obvious relationship of the person to time, and the clarity with which we perceive where his action stands in the flow of time. This is the reason the fall of the first man—which resulted in the creation of the human race—seems obviously less free than the marriage of any present-day person. This is why the life and actions of people who lived centuries ago, connected with me in time, cannot seem as free to me as the life of a living person, the consequences of which are still unknown to me.
The degree to which we perceive freedom or necessity depends in this respect on the greater or lesser gap between the performance of the action and our judgment of it.

If I examine an action I performed a moment ago under roughly the same circumstances I'm in now, my action appears undoubtedly free. But if I examine an action I performed a month ago, then—being in different circumstances—I can't help recognizing that if that act had not been committed, much of what resulted from it, good and useful, would not have taken place. If I recall an action even more remote—ten or twenty years ago—then the consequences of my action appear even more clearly, and it becomes hard for me to imagine what would have happened if that action had not occurred. The further back I go in my memories, or—what amounts to the same thing—the further forward I project my judgment, the more doubtful my notion of freedom becomes.

In history we find exactly the same progression of conviction about the role of free will in the general affairs of humanity. A contemporary event seems to us to be unquestionably the work of all the known participants. But with a more distant event, we already see its inevitable results, which prevent us from imagining anything else. And the further back we go in examining events, the less arbitrary they appear.

The Austro-Prussian War appears to us undoubtedly the result of Bismarck's cunning policies, and so on. The Napoleonic wars, though already questionably, still seem to be the product of their heroes' will. But in the Crusades we already see an event occupying its definite place in history, and without which we cannot conceive of the modern history of Europe—though the chroniclers of the Crusades saw them simply as the expression of certain people's will. Looking even further back at the migration of peoples, it occurs to no one today that the renewal of the European world depended on a whim of Attila's. The further back in history we look at the object of our observation, the more doubtful the element of free will in producing the event, and the more evident the law of necessity.

The third factor is the degree to which we grasp the endless chain of causation that reason inevitably demands, in which each comprehensible phenomenon—and therefore every human action—must have its definite place as a result of what came before and as a cause of what follows.

The better we understand the physiological, psychological, and historical laws deduced by observation—the laws by which man is governed—and the more correctly we perceive the physiological, psychological, and historical causes of the action, and the simpler the action itself, and the less complex the character and mind of the person whose action we are examining, the more subject to necessity and the less free the action appears to us.

When we do not at all understand the cause of an action—whether it is a crime, a good deed, or something morally neutral—we attribute the greatest amount of freedom to it. In the case of a crime, we most urgently demand punishment; in the case of a virtuous act, we rate its merit most highly; in the morally neutral case, we see the most individuality, originality, and independence. But if even one of the countless causes is known to us, we concede a certain amount of necessity and are less insistent in our demand for punishment, less appreciative of the virtue, and less ready to attribute freedom to the seemingly original action.

On these three factors alone is based the concept of diminished responsibility for crimes and of extenuating circumstances, as recognized by all legal codes. Responsibility appears greater or less depending on our greater or lesser knowledge of the circumstances under which the person acted, on the greater or lesser interval between the commission of the act and our judgment of it, and on our greater or lesser understanding of the causes that led to the action.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter X
paragraphs: Thus our sense of free will and necessity gradually diminishes or increases depending on the greater or lesser connection with the external world, the greater or lesser distance in time, and the greater or lesser dependence on the causes in relation to which we examine a person's life.

So if we examine the case of a person whose connection with the external world is well known, where the time between the action and our examination of it is great, and where the causes of the action are most accessible, we get a maximum sense of necessity and a minimum of free will. If we examine a person with the least possible dependence on external conditions, whose action was performed in the very recent present, and whose causes are beyond our understanding, we get a maximum sense of freedom and a minimum of necessity.

In neither case—however we shift our viewpoint, however clear we make the connection between the person and the external world, however inaccessible it may be to us, however long or short the time, however intelligible or unintelligible the causes—can we ever imagine either complete freedom or complete necessity.

(1) However much we may imagine a man to be exempt from the influence of the external world, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in space. Every human action is inevitably conditioned by what surrounds him and by his own body. I raise my arm and let it fall. My action seems free to me; but if I ask myself whether I could have raised my arm in every direction, I see that I raised it in the direction that presented the fewest obstacles. For my arm to go in a different direction, there would have needed to be fewer obstacles in that direction. For it to be completely free, it would have had to find no obstacles at all. But it is impossible to imagine a space with no obstacles. Even if I imagine a man entirely isolated from every influence, merely examining his action in the present—a momentary action without any cause—the infinitesimal remainder of necessity would still never equal zero.

(2) However closely we bring the time of judgment to the time of the deed, we never get a notion of freedom in time. For if I examine an action committed a second ago, I must still recognize it as not free, because it is irrevocably linked to the moment at which it was committed. Can I raise my arm? I raise it; but I ask myself: could I have not raised it at the moment that has already passed? To convince myself that I could have, I don't raise my arm the next moment. But the moment I was asking about was not now—it is already irrecoverably past, and the arm I then raised was in the very air through which I have now refrained from raising it. The moment in which I chose not to raise my arm is a different moment from the moment I did raise it, and the flow of time in which I chose not to act was not the same as the past flow of time in which I acted. Even if I imagine an action in the very earliest moment of the present, unevoked by any cause, the infinitesimal instant of the present as it becomes the past would still contain a minimum of necessity.

(3) However much the difficulty of understanding causes may increase, we never arrive at a notion of complete freedom—that is, an absence of cause. However inaccessible the cause of the expression of will in any action may be—our own or someone else's—the first demand of reason is the assumption of and search for a cause, because without a cause no phenomenon is conceivable. I raise my arm to perform an action that seems to me independent of any cause, but the fact that I wish to perform an action without a cause is itself the cause of my action.

But even if—imagining a man entirely free from all influences, examining only his momentary action in the present, unevoked by any cause—we were to admit so infinitely small a remainder of necessity as to equal zero, we would still not have arrived at the concept of complete freedom, because a being that is not subject to the laws of the external world, that stands outside of time and is independent of causes, is no longer a man.
In the same way, we can never imagine the action of a man completely devoid of freedom and entirely subject to the law of necessity.

(1) However much we increase our knowledge of the spatial conditions in which man exists, that knowledge can never be complete, because the number of those conditions is as infinite as infinity of space itself. And so, as long as not all the conditions influencing a man are defined, there is no complete necessity, and a certain element of freedom remains.

(2) However much we extend the period of time between the action under examination and our judgment of it, that period will always be finite, while time is infinite, and so in this respect too there can never be absolute necessity.
(3) However fully we may trace the chain of causation of any action, we will never know the whole chain, since it is endless, and so again we never reach absolute necessity.

But beyond this, even if—granting that the minimum remainder of freedom equals zero—we assumed in some given case, such as that of a dying man, an unborn child, or someone entirely bereft of reason, a complete absence of freedom, we would by doing so destroy the very concept of man in the case we are examining. For as soon as there is no freedom, there is no man. And so to imagine a man's action as entirely subject to the law of necessity, without any freedom, is just as impossible as imagining a man's action as entirely free.

To imagine a person's action as entirely subject to the law of necessity, without any freedom, we would need to know an infinite number of spatial conditions, an infinitely long period of time, and an infinite chain of causes.
To imagine a person perfectly free and not subject to the law of necessity, we would need to imagine him completely alone, outside of space, outside of time, and free from dependence on any cause.
In the first case—if necessity were possible without freedom—we would have reached a definition of necessity by the laws of necessity itself: mere form without content.

In the second case—if freedom were possible without necessity—we would have arrived at unconditional freedom beyond space, time, and cause, which by the fact of being unconditional and unlimited would be nothing—mere content without form.
We would, in fact, have reached those two foundations on which all of man's understanding of the universe is built—the incomprehensible essence of life, and the laws defining that essence.

Reason says: (1) Space, with all the forms of matter that give it visibility, is infinite and cannot be imagined otherwise. (2) Time is infinite motion without a moment of rest and is unthinkable otherwise. (3) The chain of cause and effect has no beginning and can have no end.

Consciousness says: (1) I alone am, and all that exists is merely me; therefore I include space. (2) I measure flowing time by the fixed moment of the present in which alone I am conscious of myself as living; therefore I am outside time. (3) I am beyond cause, for I feel myself to be the cause of every expression of my life.
Reason gives expression to the laws of necessity. Consciousness gives expression to the essence of freedom.
Freedom unlimited by anything is the essence of life in man's consciousness. Necessity without content is man's reason in its three forms.
Freedom is the thing examined. Necessity is what examines. Freedom is the content. Necessity is the form.
Only by separating the two sources of knowledge—related to one another as form to content—do we get the mutually exclusive and separately incomprehensible concepts of freedom and necessity.
Only by uniting them do we get a clear picture of human life.
Apart from these two concepts, which in their union mutually define one another as form and content, no conception of life is possible.
All that we know of human life is merely a certain relationship between free will and necessity—that is, between consciousness and the laws of reason.
All that we know of the external world of nature is only a certain relationship between the forces of nature and necessity—that is, between the essence of life and the laws of reason.

The great forces of nature lie outside us and we are not conscious of them. We call those forces gravity, inertia, electricity, animal force, and so on. But we are conscious of the force of life in man, and we call that freedom.

But just as the force of gravity—incomprehensible in itself but felt by every person—is understood by us only to the extent that we know the laws of necessity to which it is subject (from the first knowledge that all bodies have weight, up to Newton's law), so too the force of free will—incomprehensible in itself but felt by everyone—is understood by us only to the extent that we know the laws of necessity to which it is subject (from the fact that every man dies, to the knowledge of the most complex economic and historical laws).
All knowledge is merely a bringing of this essence of life under the laws of reason.

Man's free will differs from every other force in that man is directly conscious of it. But in the eyes of reason it is no different from any other force. The forces of gravity, electricity, or chemical affinity are distinguished from one another only in that they are differently defined by reason. In the same way, the force of man's free will is distinguished from other forces only in that reason defines it differently. Freedom without necessity—that is, without the laws of reason that define it—is no different from gravity, or heat, or the force of vegetation. For reason, it is only a momentary, undefinable feeling of life.

And just as the undefinable essence of the force that moves the heavenly bodies, the undefinable essence of heat, electricity, chemical affinity, or the vital force, forms the content of astronomy, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and so on, so the force of free will constitutes the content of history. But just as the subject of every science is the manifestation of this unknown essence of life while that essence itself can only be the subject of metaphysics, so too the manifestation of the force of free will in space, in time, and in its dependence on causes constitutes the subject of history, while free will itself is the subject of metaphysics.

In the experimental sciences, what we know we call the laws of necessity; what is unknown to us we call vital force. Vital force is merely an expression for the unknown remainder beyond what we know of the essence of life.

In the same way in history: what is known to us we call the laws of necessity; what is unknown we call free will. Free will is, for history, merely an expression for the unknown remainder of what we know about the laws of human life.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter XI
paragraphs: History examines the manifestations of man's free will in connection with the external world, in time, and in dependence on cause—that is, it defines this freedom by the laws of reason, and so history is a science only insofar as this free will is defined by those laws.

The recognition of man's free will as something capable of influencing historical events—that is, as something not subject to laws—is the same for history as the recognition of a free force moving the heavenly bodies would be for astronomy.

Such an assumption would destroy the very possibility of laws—that is, of any science whatever. If even a single body moves freely, then the laws of Kepler and Newton are negated and no conception of the movement of heavenly bodies any longer exists. If any single action is free, then not a single historical law can exist, nor any conception of historical events.

For history, there exist lines of the movement of human wills, one end of which is hidden in the unknown but at the other end of which man's consciousness of his will in the present moves in space, time, and dependence on cause.
The more this field of motion opens up before our eyes, the more evident the laws of that motion become. To discover and define those laws is the task of history.

From the standpoint that the science of history now occupies—on the path it currently follows, seeking the causes of events in man's free will—a scientific formulation of those laws is impossible. For however much man's free will may be restricted, as soon as we recognize it as a force not subject to law, the existence of law becomes impossible.

Only by reducing the element of free will to the infinitesimal—that is, by treating it as an infinitely small quantity—can we convince ourselves of the absolute inaccessibility of causes, and then instead of seeking causes, history will take as its task the discovery of laws.

The search for these laws has long since begun, and the new methods of thought that history must adopt are being worked out at the same time as the old method of history is destroying itself—endlessly dissecting and dissecting the causes of phenomena.

All the sciences of man have traveled this path. Arriving at infinitesimals, mathematics—the most exact of sciences—abandons the process of analysis and enters on the new process of integrating unknown, infinitely small quantities. Abandoning the concept of cause, mathematics seeks laws—that is, properties common to all unknown, infinitely small elements.

In a different form but along the same path, the other sciences have proceeded. When Newton stated the law of gravity, he did not say that the sun or the earth has a property of attraction. He said that all bodies, from the largest to the smallest, have the property of attracting one another—that is, leaving aside the question of the cause of the movement of bodies, he expressed a property common to all bodies, from the infinitely large to the infinitely small. The natural sciences do the same: leaving aside the question of cause, they seek laws. History stands on the same path. And if history has for its subject the study of the movement of nations and of humanity, and not the description of episodes from the lives of individuals, it too must set aside the concept of causes and seek the laws common to all the equal and inseparably interconnected infinitesimal elements of free will.
